source: Rott and Gawlick (2014) Explizites oder implizites Heurismentraining - was ist besser? (Mathematica Didactica 37)
finding: Improved replication of Schoenfeld 1979 with a practice-only control and a test-only group. Explicit heuristic training beat practice with worked solutions only, which beat no training. The authors call their own sample very small and ask for a much larger follow-up.
numbers: Teacher-training students, 5 weekly sessions. Final groups: explicit n=9, practice-only n=10, test-only n=9 (28 total). Pretest groups equal (ANOVA F=1.627, p=0.217). Posttest ANOVA F=3.853, p=0.035. ANCOVA with pretest covariate F=6.593, p=0.005. Bonferroni post-hoc explicit vs practice-only p=0.043. Corrected effect sizes d: explicit vs practice 0.786, explicit vs test-only 1.438, practice vs test-only 0.640. Pre-post effect size within explicit group 0.88 (t=-2.626, p=0.015, still significant after Bonferroni); practice-only t=0.391 and test-only t=1.953 not significant. The test-only group fell from 16 to 12 points, so the posttest was harder than the pretest. Schoenfeld's original: n=7, no test-only group.
quote: Die Anzahl der Teilnehmer ist mit etwa 10 Studierenden pro Gruppe sehr gering
limits: About 10 people per group, one university, maths teacher students only (strong in maths). Pairing of twins was dropped because only 5 pairs were left. Training-session notes were recorded but not analysed. Test-only group lost 6 of 15 at posttest. No larger replication found in this search (web search budget ran out).
agent_relevance: The human effect is real but its size is uncertain (d about 0.8 with about 10 per cell). What mattered was naming the heuristic explicitly during review after solving, across tasks. For the agent: name the heuristic in the look-back step, not only apply it.

source: Meincke, Mollick, Mollick and Shapiro (2025) Prompting Science Report 2: The Decreasing Value of Chain of Thought in Prompting
finding: On GPQA Diamond, a 'think step by step' prompt gave only small average gains on dedicated reasoning models, and a loss on one. For non-reasoning models CoT raised the average but hurt the strict 'always correct' metric on 3 of 5 models. Other prompts ('think carefully', 'decompose the problem', 'weigh three solution paths') made negligible difference on GPT-4o.
numbers: 198 questions x 25 trials per condition (4,950 runs per prompt per model), temperature 0. Reasoning models, step-by-step vs direct, average rating difference: o3-mini +0.029 (p=.024), o4-mini +0.031 (p=.003), Gemini Flash 2.5 -0.033 (p=.005). At the 100%-correct metric Flash 2.5 fell 0.131 (p<.001). CoT added 20-80% time on reasoning models and 35-600% on non-reasoning models. Non-reasoning: Gemini Flash 2.0 +0.135, Sonnet 3.5 +0.117, GPT-4o-mini +0.044 (ns); against the default no-prompt arm the gains shrink to +0.062 (Flash 2.0), +0.069 (GPT-4o), and are not significant for Sonnet 3.5 and GPT-4o-mini.
quote: For dedicated reasoning models, the added benefits of explicit CoT prompting appear negligible
limits: One benchmark (multiple-choice science, not maths), one simple CoT prompt, 8 models of early 2025. The 'direct' arm forbids thinking, which is not how anyone would use a reasoning model. Extra prompt variants were tested only on GPT-4o (100 samples per question). The authors say highly customised prompts may do better. Token counts not reported, only time.
agent_relevance: Generic procedure prompts add little to reasoning models. A Polya menu must beat 'no menu' at equal tokens on a reasoning model, and this paper shows that baseline is hard to beat with generic wording. Test problem-specific cues, not generic ones.

source: Wu, Xu, Li, Sun, Zhu and Feng (2025) Mitigating Strategy-Selection Bias in Reasoning for More Effective Test-Time Scaling (TTS-Uniform)
finding: Models sampling many solutions keep picking one dominant strategy (for example algebra). Asking the model first to list abstract solution strategies, then spending the sample budget equally across them and dropping high-entropy strategies, beats plain self-consistency at the same number of samples. Gains are large on hard competition problems and tiny on easy ones.
numbers: GPT-4o-mini and GPT-4.1-mini; same sample budget k (32 or 64; 16 or 32). In 500 samples on 3 AIME problems the dominant strategy was often more than twice all the others combined. Acc@32 GPT-4.1-mini AIME 2024: self-consistency 60.0, Uniform-C(Z) 66.6, Uniform-C(F) 70.0, Uniform-F 73.3. GPT-4o-mini AIME 2025 Acc@32: SC 3.3, Uniform-C(F) 23.3. AQuA: SC 89.0 vs best 91.3 (GPT-4.1-mini). Divergence from uniform strategy use: 53.4% higher for the weaker model.
limits: Majority vote only, no verifier. Small AIME sets (30 problems each, so one problem = 3.3 points), single runs, no confidence intervals. Strategy list comes from the same model. Equal samples, not necessarily equal tokens (strategy extraction costs extra). Non-reasoning mini models.
agent_relevance: Direct support for a menu of strategies used as a diversity device at fixed budget: ask for candidate strategies first, then split attempts across them. Weak models gain most; strong models less. Entropy of answers per strategy is a cheap signal to drop unstable strategies.

source: Naik, Chandrasekaran, Yuksekgonul, Palangi and Nushi (2024) Diversity of Thought Improves Reasoning Abilities of LLMs (DIV-SE, IDIV-SE)
finding: Asking the model for several different solution approaches (algebra, elimination, state tracking, and so on), turning each into a prompt, and voting over the answers beat self-consistency at the same or lower dollar cost. A one-call variant (all approaches in one prompt) is cheaper and still better than chain-of-thought.
numbers: GPT-4 Graph Coloring: CoT 15.0, SC-10 23.0, IDIV-SE 74.0, DIV-SE 97.0. Blocksworld 3: CoT 70, SC-10 73, IDIV-SE 82, DIV-SE 94; Blocksworld 4/5: CoT 40, SC-10 41.2, IDIV-SE 57, DIV-SE 69.6. MATH counting and probability, GPT-4 zero-shot CoT: CoT 62.24, DIV-SE 79.11 (+16.87), IDIV-SE 72.00. GPT-3.5 AQuA: DIV-SE +14.23 (few-shot, base 57.48) and +16.52 (zero-shot, base 59). GPT-3.5 Blocksworld: no gain (baselines 6% and 0.6%). LLaMA-2 70B zero-shot: negligible. Meta-reasoning aggregation instead of vote: GPT-3.5 AQuA 64.47 to 67.70, GPT-4 79.90 to 79.24.
limits: GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 of 2023, no reasoning models. Majority vote, no verifier. Cost uses 2023 prices. Gains vanish when the model cannot follow the approach (GPT-3.5 on planning, LLaMA zero-shot).
agent_relevance: Second independent support that diverse approach prompts beat repeated sampling of one prompt. Also a warning: a model too weak to execute a named approach gets nothing. Gate the menu on model ability.

source: Salah and Muneer (2026) Temperature-Dependent Performance of Prompting Strategies in Extended Reasoning LLMs
finding: On olympiad-level problems with one reasoning model, plain zero-shot and chain-of-thought prompts swapped ranks across temperatures. Neither prompt dominated. The differences are within sampling noise for 39 problems.
numbers: Grok-4.1 with extended reasoning, 39 AMO-Bench problems, one response per problem per setting, 4 temperatures. Zero-shot 59.0% at T=0.4 and T=0.7. CoT 53.8% at T=0.0 and 59.0% at T=1.0. One problem is worth 2.6 points.
limits: Single model, one sample each, no tests, no confidence intervals. Low weight. Listed because it is a recent reasoning-model comparison of CoT vs plain and agrees with d02 that CoT is not reliably better.
agent_relevance: Any prompt comparison on a reasoning model needs many samples per problem and paired tests, or differences of 5 points are noise.

source: Lee et al. (2026) Llama-Polya: Instruction Tuning for LLMs based on Polya's Problem-solving
finding: Fine-tuning Llama-3.1-8B on synthetic tutoring dialogues built around Polya's four stages balanced stage use and cut premature answers. It did not measure whether solutions became more accurate. Experts said the 'look back' stage rarely sent the student back to earlier reasoning.
numbers: Stage-skipping error rate lowest for polya-v2 (0.0%) and metamath (0.4%); general-purpose base and instruct models higher; the stacked metamath then polya-v2 model also high. 6 mathematics-education experts: self-level feedback 4.22/5, task-level feedback (explaining why an answer is right or wrong) about 2.8 to 3.2/5.
limits: A tutoring tool, not a problem-solver. No accuracy outcome, 6 raters, GSM8K-derived synthetic data. Confirms K20; no new accuracy evidence.
agent_relevance: Not evidence that Polya staging improves answers. It shows that a staged understand-plan-do-look-back template is easy to imitate while the look-back step stays shallow, which is the failure the schema must test for.

source: Huang, Chen, Mishra, Zheng, Yu, Song and Zhou (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet (ICLR 2024)
finding: Asking a model to review and fix its own answer with no outside signal made accuracy go down on reasoning tasks. Reported gains from earlier work came from using the true label to decide when to stop. The model cannot reliably judge whether its own reasoning is right.
numbers: GSM8K accuracy, GPT-3.5: standard 75.9, after self-correction round 1 75.1, round 2 74.7; with oracle label 84.3. GPT-4: standard 95.5, round 1 91.5, round 2 89.0; with oracle 97.5. GPT-4-Turbo 91.5 to 88.0 (round 1) to 90.0 (round 2). CommonSenseQA GPT-3.5: 75.8 to 38.1 to 41.8. On GSM8K GPT-3.5 kept its first answer 74.7% of the time; when it changed it, it more often changed a right answer to a wrong one.
quote: LLMs cannot properly judge the correctness of their reasoning
limits: 2023 non-reasoning models, generic 'review your answer' prompts, no reasoning-model arm. Different feedback prompts (their Tables 5 and 6) did not help either. Does not test a specific what/why/does-it-help control question.
agent_relevance: A look-back or control step that adds no new information can lower accuracy. The schema should make checks concrete (recompute, test a special case, compare to a bound) and should not ask 'are you sure'.

source: Zheng et al. (2024) ProcessBench: Identifying Process Errors in Mathematical Reasoning
finding: Finding the first wrong step in a math solution gets much harder as problems get harder, and reasoning-trained models are much better at it than ordinary chat models.
numbers: 3,400 test cases, error step marked by human experts, F1 over error and correct cases. GPT-4o-0806: GSM8K 79.2, MATH 63.6, OlympiadBench 51.4, average 61.9. o1-mini: GSM8K 93.2, MATH 88.9, OlympiadBench 87.2, average 87.9. QwQ-32B-Preview: GSM8K 88.0, MATH 78.7, OlympiadBench 57.8, average 71.5. Trained process reward models generalised worse than prompted critics on hard problems.
limits: Judging someone else's finished solution step by step, not a model watching its own live attempt. Late-2024 models. Table text partly scrambled in extraction; averages read from the figure and rows.
agent_relevance: Suggests a current reasoning model can notice a dead end far better than 2023 models could, so a control step may be worth testing on one. It is not proof that periodic self-monitoring works.

source: Tyen, Mansoor, Carbune, Chen and Mak (2024) LLMs cannot find reasoning errors, but can correct them given the error location (BIG-Bench Mistake)
finding: Models were poor at pointing to the step where a chain of thought went wrong, even in clear-cut tasks. Given the true error location, the same models corrected most wrong traces (see d16). So the weak point in self-correction is finding the error, not fixing it.
numbers: 5 tasks, 3-shot prompts, exact match on the first mistake step. Best overall: GPT-4 with direct step-level prompting 52.87%. Tracking shuffled objects: GPT-4 CoT step-level 90.67 vs GPT-3.5-Turbo 19.0. Word sorting: GPT-4 34-44; GPT-3.5 11-16. Accuracy on traces with no mistake fell as the prompting method used more calls (more false alarms).
limits: Traces are from PaLM 2 on algorithmic tasks, not competition maths. 2023 models. 300 traces per task, some sampled to 15% correct.
agent_relevance: Detection of dead ends is the bottleneck, and it trades against false alarms. A control step should produce a concrete test, and its false-alarm rate must be measured, not only its hit rate.

source: Chen et al. (2025) Reverse Thinking Makes LLMs Stronger Reasoners (RevThink)
finding: Training a small model on forward reasoning plus a model-written backward question and backward reasoning improves forward-only reasoning. Backward thinking is used as a training signal and consistency check; at test time the model still reasons forward. The 'backward question' is a forward problem written from the answer.
numbers: 12 datasets, teacher Gemini-1.5-Pro, students Mistral-7B and Gemma-7B, LoRA fine-tuning. Average gain 13.53% over student zero-shot (6.84% over the best distillation baseline). Mistral-7B, 8 held-in sets average: zero-shot 50.55, Answer Aug 57.49, RevThink 63.23. GSM8K Mistral: 54.71 zero-shot, 59.08 Answer Aug, 60.88 RevThink. MATH Mistral 10.42 to 15.28.
limits: Fine-tuning, not prompting, so it does not show that a backward prompt helps a frozen model. Math gains over the strongest baseline are small (1.8 on GSM8K); the biggest gains are on commonsense and date tasks. Teacher data was filtered by verification (Table 5 shows drops without it).
agent_relevance: Supports reformulating 'work backwards' into a forward question (what question has the given quantity as its answer) rather than asking the model to reason backward. Without training, only the reformulation idea transfers.

source: Jiang, Shi, Yu, Liu, Zhang, Li and Kwok (2024) Forward-Backward Reasoning in LLMs for Mathematical Verification (FOBAR)
finding: Mask one number in the question, supply a candidate answer, and ask the model to recover the masked number. Combining this backward check with forward voting gives a small, consistent gain over self-consistency across six arithmetic datasets and three models.
numbers: Average over six sets (AddSub, MultiArith, SingleEQ, SVAMP, GSM8K, AQuA). text-davinci-003 with CoT prompt: Self-Consistency 81.4, FOBAR 83.5. text-davinci-003 ComplexCoT: SC 83.2, FOBAR 85.0, Self-Verification 78.3. GPT-3.5-Turbo CoT: SC 85.5, FOBAR 86.6 (GSM8K 81.9 to 85.1). Plain Self-Verification fell below SC in several rows.
limits: Needs a numeric quantity to mask. Uses extra backward chains, so not equal tokens to SC. Older models. Gains of 1 to 2 points on average. Table text partly scrambled in extraction.
agent_relevance: Backward reasoning works better as a verification step on a forward answer than as a way to solve. Cheap special case: substitute the answer back into the problem. Needs a token-matched comparison before adoption.

source: Qi et al. (2025) Plan before Solving: Problem-Aware Strategy Routing for Mathematical Reasoning with LLMs (PRISM)
finding: No single reasoning strategy (chain of thought, program-aided, tool-integrated, ensemble) won across problem slices. A trained router that predicts which strategy suits each problem, runs one strategy when confident and several when not, beat the best fixed strategy. The gain was larger for weaker models.
numbers: Qwen2.5-Math-7B, DeepSeek-Math-7B, Llama-3-8B; MATH500, GSM8K, AQuA-RAT, SVAMP, ASDiv. Average gain over best single strategy: +0.9 (Qwen), +2.9 (DeepSeek), +7.6 (Llama-3-8B). MATH: 53.2% vs best single (TIR), +3.1; +2.5 over the ensemble baseline. Qwen2.5-Math-7B MATH500 pass@1: CoT 21.2, PAL 30.4, ToRA 41.4, PRISM 46.2. AQuA: CoT 37.0, PAL 18.1, ToRA 47.2, PRISM 42.1 (router did not win). SVAMP: PAL 13.5 vs PRISM 91.8.
limits: Router trained on its own multi-strategy preference data (MathStrat); strategies are CoT/code/tool, not Polya heuristics. The 'Hybrid' ensemble baseline scores are strangely low (24.0 on GSM8K), so the ensemble comparison is weak. Under-review preprint, 7-8B models, no confidence intervals.
agent_relevance: Evidence that problem features can predict which strategy to use, but only with a trained predictor. A hand-written rule (the schema's preconditions) is untested here. Per-strategy variance (13.5 to 95.3 for one strategy) shows the cost of picking wrong.

source: Gunasekara and Ratnayake (2025) Effects of structure on reasoning in instance-level Self-Discover
finding: A reasoning plan written in plain language beat the same plan forced into JSON, on MATH by 12 points and 9 points for two large open models. Making the plan fresh for each problem helped on a mixed benchmark and hurt on a uniform one, compared with one plan found once for the whole task.
numbers: MATH, 200 problems, 1-shot plan guidance. LLaMA-3.1-405B: structured JSON 63.5, unstructured 75.5 (+18.9% relative). Mistral-Large: 67.5 vs 76.5 (+13.3% relative). BBH (27 tasks) LLaMA: task-level SELF-DISCOVER 86.59, instance-level structured 85.05, unstructured 87.27; Mistral 82.04 / 83.14 / 85.57. T4D (rebuilt by the authors) LLaMA: task-level 100.00 vs instance-level 73.23 (structured) and 78.90 (unstructured).
limits: Non-reasoning open models, no repeats, MATH subsample of 200 (one problem = 0.5 point), T4D rebuilt from ToMi. The task-level arm has no unstructured version, so format and granularity are partly mixed. Does not separate failures of choosing the plan from failures of executing it.
agent_relevance: Write the plan and operator menu in prose, not rigid schema fields. Choose per-problem or per-task-type planning on task uniformity: if problems are alike, one reusable plan can beat a fresh plan each time.

source: Ge et al. (2025) Innate Reasoning is Not Enough: In-Context Learning Enhances Reasoning LLMs with Less Overthinking
finding: Contradicts d02. On distilled DeepSeek-R1 models (1.5B to 32B), zero-shot and few-shot CoT prompts raised math accuracy in most cases and cut redundant reflection sharply. Gains were big on hard problems for large models and on easy problems for small models.
numbers: Six maths sets (GSM8K, ASDiv, SAT-MATH, MATH, AIME24, AMC23). In 72% of model-by-dataset cases CoT prompting improved over direct prompting. R1-32B: gains up to 23.1% (as low as 0.6%) on easy sets, 33% to 333% relative on MATH, AIME24 and AMC23. In one hard setting R1-32B reflections per instance fell from 414.2 to 2.56 while accuracy rose from 10% to 43.3%. One-shot CoT beat few-shot CoT.
limits: The 'direct' baseline lets the model emit very few thinking tokens (many under 30), so it measures a broken mode more than ordinary use. Distilled small models, not frontier. Relative percentages on tiny bases (3.3% on AIME) look huge. Table text scrambled in extraction, so only text-stated figures used. AIME sets are 30 problems.
agent_relevance: Cautions against reading d02 as 'prompts never help'. A prompt that limits wasted reflection may matter for small reasoning models. Any menu test should log thinking tokens, not only accuracy.

source: Hembree (1992) Experiments and relational studies in problem solving: a meta-analysis (J. Research in Mathematics Education 23(3), 242-273)
finding: Abstract read only (via Crossref and the ERIC record). Full text and effect-size tables were not reachable. Over 487 reports: no problem-solving method was clearly better in grades K-5; heuristics were mildly better in grades 6-8 and clearly better in high school. Training in drawing diagrams or sketches gave the largest gain. Teachers trained in heuristics raised student performance.
numbers: 487 reports. Effect sizes by grade and method were NOT obtained. Abstract wording: heuristics 'mildly better' in grades 6-8 and 'distinctly superior' in high school; 'training for skill in such representations provided the largest performance improvement'.
quote: training for skill in such representations provided the largest performance improvement
limits: Abstract only; numeric effect sizes unavailable (publisher page returned 403). Dated study mixing many designs. Gap 5 stays open for numbers.
agent_relevance: The one strong signal in the abstract that fits the schema is representation (draw a figure or table) as the biggest lever. A reason to test diagram or table construction first.

source: Tyen et al. (2024) BIG-Bench Mistake, backtracking experiment (same paper as d09)
finding: When a model is told the true error step and regenerates from just before it, wrong traces are often fixed and a few right traces are broken. A random location also helps wrong traces but breaks more right ones. Backtracking stayed useful with a small trained locator rather than gold labels.
numbers: Absolute change in answer accuracy over 5 tasks (PaLM 2 traces). With true location: wrong-to-right +18.04 to +43.92 points; right-to-wrong -0.00 to -11.43. With random location: wrong-to-right +5.16 to +21.57; right-to-wrong -6.67 to -15.91. Losses from an imperfect locator plateau around 65% locator accuracy.
limits: Oracle labels in the main condition; traces are algorithmic puzzles with clear right answers. 2023 models. Table text scrambled in extraction, so ranges are min and max over listed task values.
agent_relevance: A mis-aimed fix costs real accuracy: random backtracking broke 7 to 16 points of correct traces. This is the measured price of a wrong or unneeded intervention, and it argues for gating any 'switch strategy' step on evidence of failure.
